canonical_definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats planning as a latent or cognitive ability of a model or agent to determine, decompose, or adapt a sequence of steps, subgoals, or actions toward a goal, often in interactive or partially observable settings and sometimes under constraints; one definition describes it as determining the sequence of actions needed to achieve a goal. Within that broad framing, some authors stress high-level natural-language plans before implementation or response generation, while others stress executable action sequences, feedback-driven adjustment, goal decomposition, constraint consideration, foresight, or feasible multi-constraint plans. A smaller line of work uses the same label for narrower behaviors, such as planning the structure of an answer before detailed generation, sequencing table operations, ordering subtasks asynchronously, evaluating candidate actions before choosing one, selecting intermediate reasoning paths, ordering graph information, or basic embodied task solving.

Space of facets. Within papers, planning is commonly broken into sub-skills such as decomposition into smaller tasks, constraint handling, foresight about outcomes, and dynamic adjustment from environmental feedback or prior actions. Papers also use nearby labels such as planning ability, planning capability, and self-planning for the same general skill, while task prioritization and action deliberation are treated as narrower facets. The same label is also used both for outlining answer content before generation and for selecting executable actions in interactive environments, so papers vary in whether the object being planned is content, operations, or actions.

Space of measurement. Planning is linked to 16 measurement instruments and 17 behavioral indicators. Among instruments, Blocksworld and TravelPlanner recur most, and the broader instrument space is mostly benchmarks or environment evaluations, with some work also using human evaluation of model-generated plans against human-created plans; among behavioral indicators, Tool use, Task decomposition, and Code generation recur most. These operationalizations line up most directly with the dominant definition of planning as multi-step, goal-directed sequencing, because papers describe planning evaluations as symbolic planning, complex multi-constraint planning, multi-step decision making, offline task planning, or plan comparison.

Links. The most recurrent link is to Reasoning: several papers claim a causal relationship from reasoning to planning, one paper claims a causal relationship from planning to reasoning, and several others report the two as related. Other repeated links involve Tool use, Task decomposition, Robustness, and World modeling: papers claim causal relationships from planning to the first three, from World modeling to planning, and in the case of Tool use, papers also report relatedness and a causal relationship from Tool use to planning. Additional papers use causal or related language for other abilities and behaviors, and no correlational links are reported.

characterization_sections.label: Space of definitions.
characterization_sections.text: Across papers, the prevailing usage treats planning as a latent or cognitive ability of a model or agent to determine, decompose, or adapt a sequence of steps, subgoals, or actions toward a goal, often in interactive or partially observable settings and sometimes under constraints; one definition describes it as determining the sequence of actions needed to achieve a goal. Within that broad framing, some authors stress high-level natural-language plans before implementation or response generation, while others stress executable action sequences, feedback-driven adjustment, goal decomposition, constraint consideration, foresight, or feasible multi-constraint plans. A smaller line of work uses the same label for narrower behaviors, such as planning the structure of an answer before detailed generation, sequencing table operations, ordering subtasks asynchronously, evaluating candidate actions before choosing one, selecting intermediate reasoning paths, ordering graph information, or basic embodied task solving.

characterization_sections.label: Space of facets.
characterization_sections.text: Within papers, planning is commonly broken into sub-skills such as decomposition into smaller tasks, constraint handling, foresight about outcomes, and dynamic adjustment from environmental feedback or prior actions. Papers also use nearby labels such as planning ability, planning capability, and self-planning for the same general skill, while task prioritization and action deliberation are treated as narrower facets. The same label is also used both for outlining answer content before generation and for selecting executable actions in interactive environments, so papers vary in whether the object being planned is content, operations, or actions.

characterization_sections.label: Space of measurement.
characterization_sections.text: Planning is linked to 16 measurement instruments and 17 behavioral indicators. Among instruments, Blocksworld and TravelPlanner recur most, and the broader instrument space is mostly benchmarks or environment evaluations, with some work also using human evaluation of model-generated plans against human-created plans; among behavioral indicators, Tool use, Task decomposition, and Code generation recur most. These operationalizations line up most directly with the dominant definition of planning as multi-step, goal-directed sequencing, because papers describe planning evaluations as symbolic planning, complex multi-constraint planning, multi-step decision making, offline task planning, or plan comparison.

characterization_sections.label: Links.
characterization_sections.text: The most recurrent link is to Reasoning: several papers claim a causal relationship from reasoning to planning, one paper claims a causal relationship from planning to reasoning, and several others report the two as related. Other repeated links involve Tool use, Task decomposition, Robustness, and World modeling: papers claim causal relationships from planning to the first three, from World modeling to planning, and in the case of Tool use, papers also report relatedness and a causal relationship from Tool use to planning. Additional papers use causal or related language for other abilities and behaviors, and no correlational links are reported.

definition_agreement.reason: Most papers define planning as the model or agent's ability to decompose a goal into an ordered, coherent sequence of steps or actions to achieve it, often in multi-step settings and sometimes with constraints, adaptation, or execution included. A few papers emphasize special cases such as natural language outlines, itinerary generation, or graph-based ordering, but these mostly read as domain-specific instantiations or added details of the same core goal-directed sequencing ability rather than a different construct.
